Domain adaptation seeks to enhance the performance of a model trained on a source domain when applied to a distinct target domain. While adversarial approaches are effective for aligning source and target distributions, they often fail to handle the inherent stochasticity of the source data. This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates adversarial and stochastic transformations to bridge source-target domain gaps while modeling data variability. By employing a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to map source samples to the target domain, we generate adversarial examples that are subsequently subjected to stochastic perturbations. These transformed samples are then used to align distributions via adversarial training. Additionally, we implement a weighted loss function to further mitigate distribution discrepancies. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques across multiple datasets.

This paper establishes that any 2-local inner derivation acting on a Jordan, associative, or Lie algebra composed of matrices over a commutative, symmetric ring $R$ is inherently an actual inner derivation. Additionally, local inner derivations on Jordan matrix algebras defined over commutative involutive rings are proven to be genuine inner derivations.

This study examines the Berry phase associated with a Dirac singularity situated at the origin within a two-dimensional plane, subject to the influence of an external magnetic field. The analysis reveals that the Aharonov-Bohm effect is modified by the field, with the resulting phase shift depending on the observer's distance from the origin. We demonstrate that this effect can be understood through path integrals of charged particles in the presence of the magnetic field, where the Diraki singularity manifests as a line flux of magnetic field perpendicular to the plane.

This study investigates the existence and stability of compactons within dense Bose-Einstein condensates influenced by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with spin-orbit coupling. We establish that compacton solutions emerge under the combined influence of the Gross-Pitaevskiev potential and the nonlinearity arising from spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, we analyze the properties of these compactons, including their width, peak amplitude, and fundamental frequency, revealing that they are highly sensitive to the spin-orbit coupling parameter.

The $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ state has been identified as a $1/2^-$ pentaquark candidate, yet its internal structure remains uncertain. This study investigates whether it corresponds to the heavy quark spin symmetry partner of the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$, a state definitively identified as a $1/2^+$ charmed-strange baryon. By analyzing the decay widths of $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ and $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ into the $D^0 K^-$ and $D^0 \bar{K}^0$ channels, we determine that $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ cannot be the heavy quark spin partner of $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$, a conclusion that supports the pentaquark hypothesis for $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$.

This study examines the equicontinuity of $G$-invariant continuous functions within the framework of topological groups acting on metric spaces. We demonstrate that the $G$-invariant $E$-sum of continuous functions defined on a metric space remains in that space, provided the functions are sufficiently $G$-uniformly continuous. Additionally, we establish that the $G$-invariant $E$-sum of $G$-equicontinuous maps is itself $G$-equicontinuous. Furthermore, we establish that the space of $G$-invariant continuous functions forms a Banach space under specific conditions.

This article outlines the potential of future muon colliders for discovering and investigating axion-like particles (ALPs). We examine the feasibility of detecting these particles through their decay into muon pairs and through the decays of virtual muons produced via ALP-mediated interactions. Our analysis indicates that, even with current theoretical uncertainties, muon colliders offer superior sensitivity to the ALP parameter space compared to existing experimental facilities. Additionally, we outline a specific search strategy for the muon colliders planned for the 2030s, focusing on the detection of both the muon pair ALPs and the A-mediated production of muon pair ALPs. Finally, we detail the computational tools and simulation frameworks employed in this study.

The increasing complexity of modern data processing systems has made it difficult to achieve high performance through single-layer optimizations. While cross-layer techniques are known to enhance performance, their practical application and evaluation remain challenging. To address this, we introduce MetaSys, an open-source, flexible system designed to implement and assess various cross-layer strategies. MetaSys offers a comprehensive framework that supports the development of custom optimizations and provides tools to measure their impact on performance. We demonstrate the system's utility by implementing and evaluating three specific techniques: (1) a data layout transformation that aligns memory access patterns with hardware capabilities, (2) a compiler pass that generates code for multiple CPU architectures, and (3) a runtime mechanism that enables dynamic offloading to GPUs. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the benefits and trade-offs associated with each method.

This paper introduces a novel transfer learning framework for image classification, leveraging synthetic data and a Siamese network. The authors first train a Siamese network using pairs of synthetic images to learn a robust, similarity-based feature representation. Subsequently, only a single image is required from the target domain to extract a feature vector via the pre-trained Siamese model. A final linear classifier, trained on these extracted features alongside image labels, completes the classification task. This approach offers a distinct advantage over traditional transfer learning methods by eliminating the need for image-to-image mapping between source and target domains. The study validates the effectiveness of this strategy through experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

This paper addresses a coupled system of two quasilinear elliptic equations, where the left-hand side features the Laplacian operators $\Delta u$ and $\Delta v$, while the right-hand side contains power-type nonlinearities $|v|^{p-1}u$ and $|u|^{q-1}u$ respectively. We establish conditions for the existence and uniqueness of positive solutions for specific ranges of the exponents $p$ and $q$. These findings are derived by applying a novel technique that transforms the system into a set of ODEs via the use of radial symmetry and an ansatz $u(r)=\lambda v(\lambda r)$.

Recurrent neural networks (RRCNs) are a class of neural networks designed to handle sequential data. However, they face a significant limitation: they struggle to learn connections between data points that are far apart in time. This issue is known as the "vanishing gradient problem." To address this, we introduce the Fourier Recurrent Unit (FRU), a new architecture that leverages Fourier series to model long-term dependencies. We demonstrate that FRUs can be seamlessly integrated into standard RNN frameworks. Experimental results show that FRUs significantly enhance the ability of RNNs to learn connections between data points that are temporally distant.

This paper introduces a new method for deriving optimal policies in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The approach is grounded in a fresh characterization of these policies, which posits that an optimal policy is equivalent to a specific set of action-value functions. The algorithm operates by identifying the policy that minimizes the distance to this target profile, utilizing a novel, polynomial-time distance metric. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this proposed distance metric is both more effective and broadly applicable than existing alternatives. Furthermore, we establish that this policy optimization problem can be resolved in polynomial time relative to the MDP's size, provided the action space is finite.

We introduce a novel method for generating attosecond electron bunches utilizing two wakefields from counter-propagating laser pulses within a plasma. This approach employs a weak, longitudinally polarized magnetic field to create a stable, circularly polarized orbit for electrons, which is then damped by the stronger wakefield. The resulting electron beam becomes linearly polarized, with its polarization plane oriented perpendicular to the main wakefield's propagation axis. Theoretical analysis of the proposed accelerator demonstrates that the beam's emittance can be reduced to approximately 100 pm$\cdot$rad. Furthermore, the longitudinal energy spread is estimated at around 100 meV, while the polarization degree reaches a saturation level of 99.9%.

This paper explores the astrophysical dimensions of life, focusing on the evolution of complexity. We examine how life has developed from simple molecules to complex organisms, emphasizing the role of astrophysical processes in this emergence. We discuss the formation of life on Earth, its potential existence elsewhere, and the challenges of detecting extraterrestrial life.

The escalating global threat of climate change has spurred a vast expansion of research, particularly within computer science, yet this surge has also triggered a fragmentation of efforts that risks duplicating work and hindering collaboration. To address this, we introduce a novel method for mapping the landscape of global climate change investigation by leveraging open-source repositories. This approach utilizes AI to analyze code repositories, a technique that has recently gained traction in the scientific community. Our study examines the advantages and constraints of this method, specifically focusing on its utility for evidence-based policy-making regarding R&D. We apply our method to map climate-related investigations within GitHub's GitLab platform, a repository that has emerged as a key source for open-source software development in recent years.

Android, the world's most widely adopted mobile platform, relies on the Android Native Development Kit (NDK) to execute performance-critical code in C and C++. This reliance on native libraries makes these applications susceptible to side-channel attacks, which can compromise the confidentiality of sensitive data. Consequently, developers must rigorously audit their native code against such threats. This paper introduces ASVAAN, a semi-automatic tool designed to assist developers in identifying side-channel vulnerabilities within NDK applications. ASVAAN operates in two phases: first, it analyzes the control flow graph of the target application to pinpoint high-risk instructions, and second, it evaluates the security implications of these instructions by analyzing the surrounding code context. To validate ASVAAN's effectiveness, we tested it on three open-source Android applications: a video player, a camera application, and a file manager. The results demonstrate that ASVAAN successfully identified several side-channel vulnerabilities that had previously gone undetected by manual security reviews.

Blockchain technology has emerged as a transformative force across numerous sectors, including finance, supply chain management, and real estate. The Ethereum blockchain, specifically, is renowned for its smart contract capabilities and the development of decentralized applications (DApps). Within this ecosystem, transactions serve as the fundamental unit of data exchange, representing the interaction between accounts. This study introduces a novel methodology for analyzing Ethereum transaction data by leveraging the blockchain's intrinsic labels. We propose a new graph-based framework that examines the temporal evolution of transaction ego networks with varying labels. This approach enables a deeper understanding of how different accounts interact with one another over time. We apply this framework to analyze the dynamic structures of ego networks for various labeled transactions. Our findings reveal that specific accounts exhibit distinct interaction patterns, offering valuable insights into their behavior and objectives. This research underscores the potential of graph-based analysis in exploring blockchain data and highlights the importance of incorporating label information to uncover nuanced interaction dynamics.

This research examines the computational complexity of linear proof search within Intuitionistic BV and Pombed logic, a domain previously unexplored. By leveraging a cut-elimination procedure derived from our prior work, we demonstrate that proof search complexity in these logics is PSPACE-complete. Furthermore, we propose a new proof of the decision property for BV and Pombed logic based on the confluence property of our zero-depth reduction system.

The Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra, first introduced by Ohtsuki in 2003, serves as a deformation of the Virasoro algebra and is defined by a set of generators and relations featuring a recursive structure. This design ensures a pentagon principle, which holds true for the $q$-deformation of the Virasoro algebra across all values of $q$. In this study, we re-examine this principle within the Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra and demonstrate its presence specifically regarding the generators' action on symmetric functions.

We introduce a novel photometric redshift algorithm, C-Phot, designed for datasets spanning 0.36 to 4.5 microns. This method employs a compulsion technique that forces the spectral energy distribution (SED) to fit the observed data points, thereby eliminating the need for arbitrary flux scaling. By utilizing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach, C-Phot generates probability density functions (PDFs) for both photometric redshifts and galaxy physical parameters. We validated the method's performance using the SDSS DR7 spectroscopic catalog, achieving a median redshift error of 0.014 and a 90th percentile error of 0.114. The algorithm was further tested on the GOODS-N field, yielding a median redshift error of 0.008 and a 90th percentile error of 0.096. We also assessed its efficacy on the GOODS-South field, which exhibits a significantly bluer average color compared to GOODS-N, observing a median redshift error of 0.006 and a 90th percentile error of 0.082. Finally, we applied C-Phot to the GOODS-S field to derive photometric redshifts for 1.2 million galaxies, demonstrating that the method successfully identifies the Lyman break and 4000 Å break, while also providing robust constraints on galaxy physical parameters.

This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for energy systems planning, designed to support decision-makers in selecting optimal alternatives. The method employs Bayesian inference to derive posterior distributions for the costs and benefits of each candidate option, which are then used to generate these choices. The decision support process is built upon a multi-criteria framework that incorporates both monetary and non-monetary factors, with the final selection determined by the weighted sum model. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a case study focused on the decarbonization of a specific region.

We introduce a minimal non-Abelian dark sector featuring a dark photon and a spin-1 dark fermion, both coupled to the Standard Model via the dark photon kinetic mixing. This framework offers an explanation for the anomalous magnetic moment of leptons by allowing the dark photon to couple to charged leptons, an interaction mediated by a mass counterterm arising from dark fermion loops. We analyze the phenomenology of this model, demonstrating that it successfully accounts for the $1\sigma$ discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment while remaining consistent with current dark photon searches and cosmological constraints.

The Digital Twin Earth (DTE) framework is a data-driven methodology designed to create a dynamic, real-time digital replica of Earth's systems. This approach integrates diverse data sources, including satellite imagery, ground sensors, and human observations, to facilitate the monitoring and analysis of environmental phenomena. A critical component of DTE is the development of "physics-informed neural operators" (PINOs), which are deep learning models trained to learn the mathematical operators governing physical processes. By capturing these underlying laws, PINOs enable the rapid simulation of physical phenomena, offering significant speed advantages over traditional numerical methods.

This study introduces a PINO-based surrogate model designed to simulate coastal flooding. The model utilizes data from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite to predict flood extents resulting from storm surges. The training dataset comprises 1,000 simulations of Hurricane Ian's impact on the Gulf of Mexico coast, featuring a grid resolution of 100 meters. The model's performance was validated against a high-resolution hydrodynamic model, demonstrating a 90% accuracy in predicting flood extent and a 50% reduction in computation time compared to conventional hydrodynamic simulations.

Cosmologlobe, a data repository for cosmology, was developed to address critical open science issues. In this study, we evaluate its effectiveness by comparing it against established standards set by BeyondPlanck, while also exploring its potential to enable reproducible research. Cosmoglobe's superior performance is evident in its streamlined data discovery and retrieval processes, which enhance both longevity and accessibility. The platform prioritizes user-friendly interfaces, prioritizing simplicity and clarity to ensure that data remains accessible to researchers. By focusing on these aspects, Cosmoglobe demonstrates its potential as a robust resource for cosmological research.

This study examines a reaction-diffusion system composed of identical Turing patterns coupled over a finite transmission line. We establish that, contrary to prior findings where coupling via finite lines invariably suppresses pattern formation, this setup can actually induce Turing instability. Specifically, a linear stability analysis reveals that for certain parameter sets, instabilities arise in a stable Turing state when the system is connected through the described network. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm these predictions and demonstrate that the resulting spatiotemporal evolution depends on the specific parameters and the initial conditions of the individual units.

We present findings from single-wire spectroscopy of both InAs and GaAs nanowires, where the wires are defined by etching the material's diameter down to approximately 100 nm. This etching process transforms the original zincblende lattice into a hexagonal wurtzite structure. Our experiments reveal that the polarization of the lowest exciton resonance in these InAs nanowires is highly sensitive to the external magnetic field. Specifically, the relative intensity of the two polarization components varies significantly with the magnetic field, a phenomenon that is distinctly absent in the corresponding GaAs nanowires. We attribute this behavior to the Zeeman splitting of the electron and hole spin states, which alters the mixing coefficients of the exciton's polarization eigenstates.

Adversary modeling is fundamental to dialogue systems, yet it remains difficult to apply in practical scenarios because adversaries are unpredictable and difficult to define. This paper introduces a new framework for adversary modeling in negotiation through data adaptation. We first construct a two-party negotiation dataset by introducing a hypothetical opponent, then employ a deep generative model to transform this related data into an adversarial counterpart that captures specific negotiation strategies. This adapted data trains a naturalistic two-party negotiation simulator. Experiments demonstrate that our approach effectively models these interactions and generates high-quality dialogues.

This study examines a specific type of compactification involving light-like portions within a six-dimensional framework. We demonstrate that this approach yields an effective five-dimensional theory featuring a dynamical string tension.

This study investigates the optimal design for sequential binary treatments, aiming to balance cumulative participant exposure to both control and intervention groups. We introduce a novel method called the Pigeonhole Design (PDS), which operates by categorizing trial participants into specific groups based on their predicted future order in the randomization sequence. Within each group, individuals are assigned to a treatment alternately, beginning with a control. This approach ensures that the final counts of participants receiving the control versus the treatment differ by no more than one. We demonstrate that PDS minimizes both the maximum and the expected absolute difference between the final treatment counts across all possible orderings. Furthermore, we analyze the PDS through the lens of online matching, establishing a theoretical framework that proves its optimality. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the PDS's performance regarding balance, bias, and efficiency in various scenarios, supported by a simulation study comparing it to existing methods. The results indicate that the PDS outperforms current designs in terms of balance and reduces the sample size required to achieve a specific balance level by approximately 10% to 20%.

The atomic-level interface between silicon and aluminum oxide remains a critical yet elusive challenge in oxide electronics. This study utilizes first-principles calculations to investigate the atomic bonding characteristics at a Si-Al$_2$O$_3$ interface, specifically examining the Si-Al and Si-O bonds. We demonstrate that the Si-Al interaction is ionic in nature, with the charge transfer from silicon to aluminum driven by the electronegativity disparity between the two elements. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the charge transfer is not a one-way process; instead, the charge accumulated on aluminum is partially offset by charge transfer from oxygen back to silicon via the Si-O bond. Consequently, the Si-O bond exhibits a mixed character, combining covalent and ionic traits. These findings offer a new perspective on the atomic bonding mechanisms at the Si-Al$_2$O$_3$ interface, providing a foundation for the design of advanced oxide electronic devices.

This study investigates the nonlinear statistical modeling of gravitational collapse, specifically focusing on the $L_1$-norm of the residual error. We establish that the collapse solution minimizing this metric is unique and possesses a continuous, differentiable nature. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the existence of a unique solution characterized by minimal Shannon entropy. We further prove that a solution with average Kullback-Leibler divergence is both unique and infinitely differentiable. These findings indicate that various information-theoretic principles yield distinctive yet analytically tractable collapse solutions for black holes.

This study introduces a comprehensive historical dataset on the global container shipping industry spanning from 1966 to the present. The data encompasses four key areas: freight rates, shipment volumes, inventories of new and scrap vessels, and prices of second-hand container ships. The series was derived from the 1966–present issues of *Containerisation International* magazine. The freight rates are categorized by shipping zones and expressed in dollars per TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit). Shipping quantities are similarly organized by zones and reported as total TEU volumes. The volume series underwent normalization to adjust for inflation and fluctuations in global trade demand. The vessel inventory series are presented in natural units, tracking the count of container ships by type (e.g., cell, non-cell) and size (e.g., TEU capacity). The dataset on second-hand and scrap prices aggregates data from multiple sources, including *Containerisation International* and *Marine Economics*, and is also adjusted for inflation. The authors provide a detailed examination of the data's characteristics, potential biases, and limitations. Additionally, the study offers a quantitative analysis of the relationships between these four data series and evaluates the impact of these factors on overall economic activity.

This study investigates the efficacy of anomaly detection systems when confronted with a diverse array of data sources. We demonstrate that a straightforward meta-level mechanism, capable of integrating predictions from multiple detectors, consistently surpasses the accuracy of any individual model tested. Our findings indicate that even the least precise detector outperforms raw data analysis, while our proposed ensemble approach yields superior results across all scenarios. Furthermore, we confirm that detector performance is heavily contingent upon the specific data set, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of various strategies for constructing such a detector ensemble.

This study introduces a novel approach for segmenting gliomas in brain MRI images by integrating a convolutional neural network (CNN) with specific post-processing methods. The system utilizes a U-Net architecture trained on 100 T1-weighted images with contrast enhancement, each annotated with 3D masks for the tumor core, enhancing tumor regions, and edema. Triplons represent the fundamental excitations in quantum antiferromagnets, serving as bosons that emerge from the coupling of spin and lattice degrees of freedom. This study examines the emergence of triplets in insulating spin-Peierls compounds, specifically CuBe₂(Po,S)₄ and CuBe₂(Se,S)₄, using inelastic neutron scattering. We observed a broad continuum of spin excitations in the energy range of 10–30 meV, which we attribute to the presence of triplons. By applying a theoretical framework that incorporates both the Bose nature of triplons and their interactions with lattice vibrations, we successfully reproduced the observed excitation spectra. This analysis yielded a triplon energy scale of approximately 10–30 meV, which aligns with the energy gap of the ground state. Furthermore, we estimated the triplon density to be roughly 10⁻⁴ cm⁻³, confirming that these excitations are present in minute concentrations within the ground state.

This paper examines the convergence of networks regarding a Moore space utilizing the framework networked sequences generalized by directed sets. This broader category encompasses sequences as a specific instance. Our findings demonstrate the equivalence between the convergence of a network and the corresponding convergence of a tailored network structured around directed sets within the text.

This study introduces two finite element methods for solving the 1D Rosenau equation: a standard discontinuous Galerkin finite element method and a novel second-order finite difference scheme based on discontinuous Galerkin finite elements. The analysis establishes the existence, uniqueness, and error estimates for these approaches, with corresponding numerical experiments conducted to validate the theoretical findings.

This study examines the stability of a coupled PDE system governing compressible and compressible fluid interactions, where the Navier-Stucker equations model the compressible phase and the Stokes equations model the incompressible phase. By applying operator-theoretical techniques, we demonstrate the well-posedness of this inf-sup weighted framework using semigroup theory.

We present a theoretical investigation into the magnetic-field-driven Wigner crystallization of charged interlayer excitons (CIEs) within van der Waals bilayers. By examining the ground state of two interacting CIEs, we determine their potential energy surfaces and identify the critical conditions for crystallization. Our results indicate that the magnetic field induces a transition from a liquid to a crystalline phase, with the critical field strength increasing as the CIE density drops. Furthermore, the interlayer separation is a decisive factor: in bilayers with a large separation, the CIEs form a triangular lattice, whereas those with a small separation form a hexagonal lattice. These findings offer a viable pathway to experimentally realize CIE crystallization and enable the manipulation of CIE states and properties in van der Waals bilayers using magnetic fields.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) has delivered a vast collection of medium-resolution radial velocity (RV) data, which is essential for investigating stellar and planetary systems. However, the raw RVs from LAMOST are subject to significant systematic errors, primarily due to the instrument's low resolution and the use of a cross-correlation method for radial velocity calculations. This study examines the main sources of systematic errors in LAMOST RVs and proposes a relative adjustment method. By comparing LAMOST RVs with Gaia DR2 proper motions, we identified a consistent positive offset of approximately 0.6 km/s. This offset is attributed to the wavelength calibration of the LAMOST Low-Resolution Spectrograph (LRS), which is responsible for the raw radial velocity data. Consequently, we developed a relative adjustment strategy to correct for this bias. This approach utilizes Gaia DR2 proper motions to calibrate LAMOST RVs, thereby mitigating the systematic offset. We applied this correction to 1,000,000 LAMOST RVs, achieving a median absolute deviation of 0.10 km/s between the adjusted values and Gaia DR2 proper motions. This correction significantly enhances the precision of LAMOST RVs, facilitating more accurate research into stellar and planetary systems.

This study addresses the inverse scattering problem for a time-harmonic wave governed by the Helmholtz equation, specifically within a medium featuring spatially varying wave speed. We introduce a deep learning approach capable of reconstructing the inverse medium from field data obtained through measurements across a wide frequency spectrum. The proposed method utilizes equivariant neural networks to model the inverse medium, leveraging multi-frequency data collected from various incident directions. This strategy is designed to enhance model generalization, thereby enabling accurate predictions of the medium at frequencies beyond those used for training. The efficacy of the method is demonstrated through numerical experiments.

This study introduces a new, cost-effective method for accelerated degradation testing (e.g., battery capacity loss) by accounting for correlations between test units. The approach utilizes a bivariate gamma process with dependency to model degradation trajectories for each unit. By leveraging the inverse relationship between the estimated degradation curves and the number of test units, we determine the optimal sample size required to achieve a specific level of precision regarding mean degradation. The proposed model was validated using both simulated data and a real-world dataset from battery tests. Results indicate that this approach yields lower testing costs compared to existing methods.

This study examines the thermodynamic properties of solar wind plasma within the CME core, specifically focusing on the interaction between CMEs and High-Speed Streams (HSS). We analyze 100 events involving HSS and CME interactions, alongside 100 non-interacting CME events, to determine the polytropic index ($\gamma$) and compare their distributions. Our findings reveal that CME plasma in interaction events exhibits a significantly higher polytropic index than those occurring without interaction. We hypothesize that this increase arises from the mixing of CME plasma with the HSS, which is characterized by a lower $\gamma$ value.

This paper introduces a new R package designed to facilitate the simulation of the Random Waypoint Mobility Model (RWMM) for mobile entities. The RWMM represents a basic stochastic approach for generating stochastic trajectories for such entities. The package includes functions for generating, visualizing, and analyzing these paths, as well as for saving and loading them. The methods used to generate these paths are explained, and various simulation scenarios are presented to demonstrate the package's capabilities.

The microscopic collective inertial mass, a crucial component of the many-body collective Hamiltonian, is calculated using the Cranking approximation. This calculation incorporates the effective nucleonic mass ($m^*$) and the density of single-particle states ($g$) as functions of the nuclear density, $\rho$. Our results demonstrate that the collective inertial moment, denoted as $\mathcal{M}_{\text{coll}}$, is directly proportional to $g$ and inversely proportional to $m^*$. This relationship indicates that the collective inertial moment is significantly enhanced by both a higher density of single-particle states and a lower value of the nucleonic effective mass.

This paper outlines the creation of the Representation and Reasoning (R&R) Corpus, a collection of 100 papers focused on graph-based constraints. The corpus targets a niche domain at the intersection of graphical and constraint representation with deductive reasoning. Its primary goal is to foster research on new graphical methods for expressing and solving reasoning tasks, thereby advancing the broader fields of graphical representation and constraint logic programming. To achieve this, we introduce a novel graph-based formalism for handling relational constraints, present a comprehensive survey of existing graphical representation and search methodologies, and provide practical examples illustrating how specific problems are encoded and solved using these techniques.

This study investigates the regularity properties of solutions to conservation laws featuring discontinuous flux, specifically addressing the regularity of gradients and higher-order derivatives. We demonstrate that solutions exhibit fractional Sobolev regularity with parameters $\frac{1}{2}$ for the first derivatives and $\frac{1}{3}$ for the second derivatives. These regularity bounds are confirmed through various numerical experiments, which also include a comparative analysis of these findings against current theoretical literature.

This study reports measurements of the branching fractions for $B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ and $B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}$ decays, utilizing data from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV collected by the LHCb detector with an integrated luminosity of $3.0$ fb$^{-1}$. The determined branching fractions are $\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}) = (1.02 \pm 0.10 \pm 0.05) \times 10^{-4}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}) = (2.12 \pm 0.12 \pm 0.06) \times 10^{-4}$, where the first uncertainties are statistical and the second are systematic.

This study examines a multicarrier-division duplex (MCDD) cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) system featuring a multi-antenna access point (AP) architecture. In this setup, uplink and downlink transmissions occur across distinct multicarriers, with the CF-mMIMO comprising numerous spatially dispersed APs serving users via a shared radio frequency spectrum. The research investigates the spectral efficiency (SE) of this system, accounting for intercarrier interference (ICI) and interference from other cells. By applying a large system analysis, we derive the SE lower bound for the MCDD-CF-mMIMO framework. The results indicate that the proposed approach offers a superior lower bound on the CF-mMIMO SE compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MCDD-CF-mMIMO system delivers higher performance than the frequency-division duplex (FDD) counterpart, particularly in scenarios with a limited number of APs.

Differential Privacy (DP) is a rigorous framework for quantifying privacy risks in data analysis. The Shuffle Model, a recent advancement, offers heightened privacy assurances by obscuring individual user identities during the data collection phase. This paper introduces \emph{strict accounting}, a methodology for precisely tracking DP noise within this model. We apply this approach to prove tight lower bounds on the minimal noise necessary for fundamental operations, including sampling and computing statistical metrics. Additionally, we establish a general strict accounting protocol for various private mechanisms and present a new \emph{shuffle-and-add} mechanism that achieves optimal noise performance for specific scenarios.

Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is a prevalent modulation technique in wireless communications, yet it lacks inherent robustness against Doppler shifts. To address this limitation, Orthogonal Time Frequency Multiplexing (OTFS) was introduced as an advanced successor. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the OTFS framework, covering its fundamental principles, system architecture, and performance characteristics. We also detail a low-complexity OTFS receiver design utilizing a subspace-based approach. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this proposed receiver achieves performance nearly identical to that of Maximum Likelihood (ML) detection while maintaining significantly reduced computational complexity.

We introduce a novel method for approximating the probability that a random assignment satisfies a given DNF formula, demonstrating that this approach yields a constant-factor approximation for DNF expressions and a nearly $O(1/\epsilon)$-approximation for DNFs, where $\epsilon$ is the target error tolerance. This performance surpasses the previously established best constant-factor bounds. Additionally, we demonstrate that a DNF formula can be transformed into an equivalent CNDN formula with an $\epsilon$-error margin in a runtime of $2^{O(n\log n\epsilon)}$, thereby achieving a constant-factor approximation for CNF formulas.

Bistability is a fundamental concept in systems biology, defined by a model's capacity to settle into two distinct stable states in response to specific inputs. This paper introduces a novel methodology for detecting bistability in continuous-time, high-dimensional, and complex dynamical systems. The approach leverages the Conley index, a topological tool that provides a coarse approximation of a system's attractor. By employing this index, the method identifies bistability by demonstrating the absence of a connecting orbit between the two attractors. The validity of this approach is confirmed through various numerical experiments, alongside its application to real-world biological models.

This study examines the structure of spin-aligned strange quark stars under finite temperature conditions and strong magnetic fields. Utilizing the MIT bag model, we establish the equation of state for spin-isolated degenerate quark matter, specifically accounting for the influence of the magnetic field. Subsequently, we determine key stellar characteristics, including mass, radius, and the central energy density, to analyze their behavior in relation to varying magnetic intensity, temperature, and spin polarization.

Audio-visual correlation detection involves identifying temporal correspondences between audio and video content, a task with significant potential for numerous downstream applications. This work reviews recent advancements in audio-visual correlation learning powered by deep neural networks. We begin by examining the specific challenges inherent to this domain, followed by a systematic classification of existing methods into three categories: (1) learning representations for audio and video independently, (2) learning representations that explicitly encode correlations, and (3) learning to predict correlations directly. We conclude by discussing several critical obstacles within audio-visual correlation detection and outline potential avenues for future research.

The Linear Ordering Problem (LOP) is a well-known issue in combinatorial optimization that seeks to identify a linear arrangement of a set of items to maximize the proportion of correct pairwise comparisons. This paper investigates the dependability of solutions within the LOP framework, treating it as a stochastic programming task. We introduce a novel probabilistic model that accounts for uncertainty in pairwise data, alongside new algorithms designed to find robust solutions. Our approach is validated through experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating the practical utility of the proposed methods.

We examine the phase-fluctuation phenomena in NbN superconducting nanofilms, which exhibit significant granularity. By analyzing the temperature dependence of the upper-critical field ($H_{c2}(T)$) and the superconducting gap ($\Delta(T)$), we observe that the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) is markedly suppressed in these nanofilms compared to their bulk counterparts. This $T_c$ reduction correlates with a decrease in the mean free path, a condition that intensifies phase fluctuations. Furthermore, we identify a distinct $H_{c2}$ behavior in the normal-to-superconducting regime, which aligns with a theoretical model incorporating granularity and phase fluctuations. Additionally, we document a non-monotonic temperature variation in the superconducting gap, a feature that can be accounted for by a model that integrates phase fluctuations with the effects of granularity.

This paper presents Temporal Trianl Queries (TTQs), an extension of regular trail queries designed for temporal graphs. In these structures, edges are labeled with specific time intervals, and the objective is to identify trails—sequences of edge-disjoint edges—linking two nodes while ensuring their time labels do not overlap. The study provides a theoretical analysis of TTQs, detailing their syntax, semantics, and associated complexity. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm optimized for computing TTQs, which is evaluated against existing methods through extensive experiments on real-world datasets.

This study introduces a novel method for decelerating polyatomic free radicals using a lithium atom beam, driven by the formation of a stable Li-C$_60$ complex. The process involves two distinct stages: first, the polyatomic free radical combines with a decelerated lithium beam within a beam-beam interaction region to create a Li-radical complex; second, this complex undergoes Zeeman deceleration to reach its final low velocity. The research successfully demonstrated the production of the C$_60$-Li complex, which was observed via a mass spectrometer. This technique offers a pathway to generate polyatomic free radicals at velocities as low as 100 m/s, enabling the study of their chemical reactions and physical properties.

The Swift-XRT catalogue of variable sources, updated continuously, is presented. This compilation includes all X-ray transients detected by the Swift satellite, covering the period from its launch in 2004 until 2022. The dataset encompasses 11,000 transient events, with 10,000 identified by the Real-Time Transient Identification (RTTI) algorithm. The RTTI system automatically detects and flags X-ray transients in real-time, utilizing a method based on a neural network to analyze light curve variability. The catalogue also incorporates 10,000 additional transient events that were not flagged by the system, including those missed due to data gaps, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to low variability, or those missed due to

We investigate the spin-1/2 J1-J2 XY model on a square lattice, which features competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interactions. By employing both exact diagonalization and density matrix renormalization group methods, we analyze the ground state phase diagram. Our results indicate that the phase diagram comprises four distinct regions: a plaquette valence bond phase, a Néel antiferromagnetic phase, a polarized ferromagnetic phase, and a resonance valence bond phase. Specifically, the plaquette valence bond phase emerges from competing interactions between nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor bonds, existing between the resonating valence bond and Néel antiferromagnetic phases. This phase is characterized by the coexistence of both short-range Néel and long-range valence bond ordering. Furthermore, we determine the phase boundaries for the plaquette valence bond state using the fidelity susceptibility, which exhibits a unique signature: the susceptibility diverges at the transition to the valence bond phase, whereas it remains finite at the transition to the resonating valence bond state.

This study introduces a decomposition framework for bilateral exchange flows utilizing a three-dimensional panel data model. The primary advantage of this approach is its ability to separate the distinct dynamics of individual trading pairs from those of specific exporter or "importer" counterparts. By applying this method to 2002–2020 data on China's exports and imports, we identify that bilateral exchange flows are driven by three main components: a common trend shared across all relationships, exporter-specific effects, and importer-specific effects. Our findings indicate that while the common trend accounts for a substantial portion of the total flow volume, the exporter and importer specific effects are equally critical, with the latter two components displaying distinct dynamics. Furthermore, we analyze the time-varying behavior of these components to assess their impact on China's trade structure. The results suggest that the common trend and exporter effects have been the primary drivers of the shift toward a services trade orientation, whereas the role of the importer-specific component has been relatively minor.

This study examines the noncommutative modification of $U(1)$ gauge theory in four dimensions, specifically addressing the challenges posed by Moyal products. We demonstrate that this noncommutative framework can be reinterpreted as a standard field theory in four dimensions, provided one accepts a specific non-trivial $L_{\infty}$ structure. The resulting $L_{\infty}$ algebra is non-greissian and non-symmetric, with its defining brackets defined recursively through the Moyal products. Furthermore, we establish a direct link between the noncommutative $U(1)$ theory and the $L_{\infty}$-based formulation of the 4D Born-Infeld action, revealing that the Moyal products in this context are generated via the recursive application of the Born-Infeld bracket.

This study addresses the equalization of linear quantum systems, aiming to reconstruct a quantum input signal from a quantum output. We propose a generalization of the Wiener filter, suitable for linear quantum systems, to achieve this equalization. This proposed filter is shown to be equivalent to the solution of the equalization problem within a generalization of the Wiener-Mosely framework. We further prove that a stable filter solution exists under the generalization of the LeGat conditions. Finally, the equalization problem is applied to the quantum communication field, demonstrating its utility in equalizing quantum channels.

Time perception is a vital cognitive function that can serve as an indicator of mental health. This study introduces a wearable-based approach to continuously assess the duration of time perception by analyzing physiological signals. The proposed method involves collecting data from wearable devices and utilizing a machine learning model to estimate the perceived time length. This estimation process comprises two main steps: first, a clustering algorithm groups similar physiological signal patterns, and second, a regression model predicts the time perception duration for each cluster. The system was evaluated using data from 20 participants who completed time perception tasks while wearing smartwatches. Results indicate that the estimation accuracy is strongly influenced by the number of participants assigned to the machine learning model, with higher accuracy achieved when more subjects are incorporated into the training set.

This study investigates the trade-off between decision quality and speed in the field, utilizing data from 1,000 experienced restaurant servers. The research examines how service time impacts tip earnings, leveraging the natural variation in decision complexity and the natural time limits imposed by customer dining. The findings indicate that faster service results in lower tips, yet this penalty is not uniform across all orders. Specifically, the speed-quality trade-off is more severe for complex decisions, such as those involving multiple diners, whereas the impact of speed on simple decisions, like those for a single diner, is minimal. These results suggest that the extent to which rushing compromises the quality of complex decisions is contingent upon their inherent level of complexity.

The growing integration of machine learning into critical sectors like healthcare and finance has intensified the need to ensure these systems are fair. While numerous fairness definitions have been proposed, legal scholars have yet to evaluate their consistency with U.S. legislation. This study bridges that gap by analyzing the alignment between established fairness definitions and U.S. fair lending laws. We demonstrate that certain definitions conflict with specific U.S. regulations, whereas others remain legally grounded. Additionally, we offer a U.S. legal perspective to refine existing fairness definitions, suggesting an ideal definition that satisfies both U.S. laws and EU standards. Ultimately, we argue that grounding fairness definitions in U.S. laws ensures their compatibility with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

This study introduces a novel method for detecting neutrino pair discharge (NPD) by utilizing the magnetic anisotropy of trivalent lanthanide ions. The proposed approach relies on the spin-orbit coupling of these ions, which creates a significant magnetic anisotropy that can be observed through magnetization measurements. The population of the ions' excited states is achieved via neutrino pair discharge, and the resulting magnetization anisotropy is measured to identify the NPD signal. Theoretical calculations indicate that the magnetization anisotropy resulting from NPD is substantial enough to be detected experimentally.

This study investigates strangeness hypernuclei ranging from $A=3$ to $A=8$ using the framework of efficient field theory. We employ a chiral effective field theory to construct the Hamiltonian, incorporating interactions between nucleons and kaons. The model's parameters are calibrated against empirical binding energies for $A=3, 4, 5,$ and $8$ hypernuclei, with the final parameter set applied to predict the binding energies of $A=3, 4, 5,$ and $8$ double-strangeness systems. Our findings indicate that single-strangeness hypernuclei exhibit a predominantly $A$-independent binding energy per particle, whereas double-strangeness hypernuclei show a binding energy per particle that scales linearly with $A$.

This paper introduces MetaPriv, a browser extension designed to assist social media users in safeguarding their privacy. MetaPriv offers a comprehensive suite of tools, including automated detection of tracking pixels, ad blockers, customizable notification alerts, and extensive user preferences for managing privacy settings. Additionally, the extension provides a centralized hub for managing subscriptions and follows the GDPR framework to ensure users can easily comply with their right to be forgotten.

We investigate the coalescent point process associated with an ancestral lineage of an age-dependent branching process evolving in changing environmental conditions. This lineage's history is governed by time-varying birth and death rates, which are themselves functions of the population size. We establish sufficient conditions for this coalescent process to converge in distribution to specific limiting processes, including the Poisson process, the uniform binary coalescent, the uniform polytomic coalescent, and the uniform multinomial coalescent.

The hierarchical conditional model (HCM) was originally introduced by Maes and Zahariev in 1991 to study the Potts model within the context of a mean-field approximation. In this study, we examine the behavior of the spin variables in the HCM under the condition that the number of spin states is infinite. We demonstrate that for sufficiently low temperatures, the HCM exhibits an uncountable collection of Gibbs measures, with the spins taking values from the unit circle. Furthermore, we establish that the HCM lacks specification, meaning it fails to satisfy the specification property.

This study presents a catalog containing central velocity dispersion ($\sigma_0$) measurements for 1,005 early-type galaxies (ETGs) drawn from the LAMOST-DR7 dataset. The $\sigma_0$ values were derived using the Emission-Line Fitting (ELF) technique, which utilizes the spectral range 4800–5500 Å to identify H$\beta$ and [O III] emission lines. The catalog's reliability is confirmed through comparisons with existing $\sigma_0$ data from SDSS-DR7, 2MASS, and the 2dF catalog. The catalog's completeness is evaluated against the SDSS-DR7 ETG sample, revealing that 97% of the LAMOST-DR7 ETGs have counterparts in the SDSS-DR7 catalog. The catalog's utility is demonstrated by analyzing the $\sigma_0$–$M_{\rm B}$ and $\sigma_0$–$M_{\rm BH}$ relations, where the latter relies on black hole mass estimates from the $M_{\rm BH}$–$\sigma_0$ correlation.

This study introduces a computational framework for calculating nuclear reaction corrections to atomic energy levels, specifically targeting isotope shifts in atomic indium. The methodology employs the relativistic coupled-cluster (RCPC) approach, utilizing a coupled-pair approximation to account for correlated electron interactions. The study demonstrates that the RCPC method achieves high precision in calculating energy levels, with deviations from experimental values remaining below 0.05 cm⁻¹. The authors also highlight the importance of including the recoil correction, which is found to be significant for isotope shifts. The study concludes that the RCPC method, combined with recoil correction, is a powerful tool for calculating isotope shifts and can be used to determine nuclear mass differences with high precision.

This study examines the variety of principal minors within the positive semidefinite adjacency matrices of graph states. Graph states are quantum arrangements derived from an underlying graph, where each node corresponds to a qubit. We demonstrate that this variety of principal minors uniquely and precisely reconstructs the underlying graph. Specifically, we present an algorithm that reconstructs the graph with a time complexity of $O(m^{3}n^{2})$, defined by $m$ edges and $n$ vertices. Furthermore, we establish upper bounds on both rank deficiency and the number of distinct zero-valued principal minors. Additionally, we prove that for graph states originating from tree structures, the variety of principal minors exhibits significant diversity.

A transversal is defined as a selection of exactly one element from each of the sets in a family of pairwise disjoint subsets of a set $X$. The existence of such a transversal is guaranteed when the family of sets is finite and all sets have equal cardinality. This paper generalizes that result to the case where the family of sets is countably infinite, provided that each set has either a finite or a countably infinite cardinality.

The surge in demand for video streaming has driven the need for transcoding, a process that converts video into various formats and qualities to ensure compatibility with diverse devices and network conditions. While cloud environments have become the preferred solution for delivering transcoding services, their heterogeneous nature—characterized by a mix of resources with varying capabilities—makes it challenging to determine optimal resource allocation for specific tasks. This study introduces a methodology for evaluating and modeling video transcoding within heterogeneous cloud settings. It begins by developing a transcoding model that accounts for both the inherent properties of the input video and the computational features of the resources. Subsequently, it calculates the necessary resources and execution time for transcoding a specific video using this model. Finally, it evaluates service performance by running actual transcoding jobs across multiple cloud resources and contrasting the results with the theoretical predictions derived from the model.

This study examines the impact of cycle count variations on the performance of a single-core and a multicore system, where the latter executes a fraction of instructions per cycle compared to the former. We demonstrate that a minor 10% reduction in cycles per cycle in the multicore environment can achieve a 100% speedup in computational tasks, provided core count remains constant. Furthermore, we illustrate that a multicore system operating at the same cycle count as a single-core machine can handle 10 times more instructions per cycle while maintaining identical overall performance. These findings indicate that cycle count metrics are unreliable for evaluating computational efficiency in multicore architectures.

This work examines the ground state solution to the energy ultracritical three-dimensional Gross--Pitaevskii equation, defined by $\Delta u+|u|^2u-\Delta^2 u=0$ for $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. We establish that this solution, denoted as $u_\lambda$, possesses a Morse index of 3, indicating it is the ground state. This finding resolves an open question posed by Wei and Yan in \cite{WeiYan2019}.

The Full-Duplex Radio (FDR) represents a groundbreaking technology designed to transmit and receive data on the same frequency band simultaneously, thereby doubling spectral efficiency. Despite its promise, FDR operation is hindered by self-interference caused by the transmitter's signal leaking into its own receiver. This interference can be mitigated through a combination of spatial, analog, and digital methods. This study presents a novel framework for Self-Interference Cancellation (SIC) that integrates advanced multi-antenna techniques with multiple SIC stages. This approach leverages the spatial diversity inherent in FDR systems to enhance interference suppression capabilities. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed SIC framework achieves an average Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR) of 100 dB, outperforming traditional single-stage SIC methods by 10 dB.

Collapsing liquid droplets are a common occurrence in nature, with their infolding dynamics playing a crucial role in biological processes such as embryogenesis. This study investigates the collapse of small (100–200 µm) droplets composed of colloidal particles suspended in a solvent. We demonstrate that the droplets' shape is governed by the interplay between capillary forces and the mechanical properties of the colloidal matrix. During the initial collapse phase, the fluid drains from the center, causing the droplet to form a spherical cap. Subsequently, buckling occurs at the base, leading to an increase in height and a reduction in the base radius. This study investigates the impact of UV radiation on the chemical and thermal state of gas within protoplanetary disks. We developed a 2D radiative transfer model that incorporates UV fluorescence and self-shielding effects to simulate the evolution of the H2, CO, and Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) line emissions. Our results indicate that the UV flux is strong enough to dissociate H2 and CO molecules in the disk's upper layers, creating a depletion zone. The extent of this H2-depleted region is governed by the UV flux intensity and the optical depth of the disk. Additionally, we observed a significant correlation between Ly$\alpha$ emission and UV flux, which allows astronomers to use Ly$\alpha$ as a proxy for estimating UV radiation levels. We also analyzed the relationship between UV flux and dust temperature, finding that the UV flux is the primary driver of dust temperature evolution in the disk's upper layers. Consequently, dust temperature can serve as an indicator of UV radiation intensity. Finally, we demonstrated that the UV flux is likely to be higher in the inner disk regions compared to the outer disk, which has important implications for the formation and evolution of planets.

This paper introduces a new fingerprint-based millimeter wave (mmWave) localization framework enhanced by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). The proposed architecture leverages a RIS to generate multiple line-of-sight (LoS) paths, thereby increasing the number of available reference points for creating a positioning fingerprint database. This expanded dataset significantly improves the accuracy of the fingerprint matching process. The study further examines how the deployment of the RIS influences localization performance, specifically analyzing the trade-offs between increasing the count of reference points and optimizing RIS element placement. The findings demonstrate that mmWave localization accuracy can be substantially enhanced by expanding the number of LoS paths through RIS assistance.

We investigate the generation of twisted particles within constant electromagnetic fields utilizing the Wilson loop framework. Our analysis demonstrates that twisted states can emerge from virtual particle production in such fields, where an external magnetic field ensures the persistence of twist via a twisting mechanism. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between twisted particles and skyrmions in the context of the massless Schwinger model.

The surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption is driving a corresponding demand for charging infrastructure, necessitating a re-evaluation of how this infrastructure is deployed, priced, and managed within the market. This paper introduces a framework designed to optimize charging network placement, pricing strategies, and market dynamics. The study begins by formulating an optimization model to identify optimal charging station locations that maximize the number of serviceable EVs, followed by a proposed mechanism to price these stations. This pricing mechanism is constructed to be individually rational and strategy-proof, ensuring fair participation. Furthermore, we develop a market model that facilitates trading between charging service providers and EV owners, incorporating a specific auction design for this interaction. The effectiveness of the proposed models is validated through extensive numerical simulations.

This study introduces a general mathematical framework for analyzing optimal tie-breaker mechanisms, which are utilized in various fields including sports, academia, and elections. We begin by establishing an abstract model for these mechanisms, followed by a detailed examination of two prominent categories: those that are monotonic and those that are "best-of" in nature. We formulate specific criteria for optimality within these categories and demonstrate that our proposed concepts align with existing definitions in the literature. Furthermore, we introduce novel examples of optimal mechanisms, including those that are best-of and monotonic.

This study investigates three-point correlation functions within $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal theories, specifically focusing on higher-spin spinor current multiplets. We establish the structure of these functions in a general setting and derive specific formulas for particular cases, including the three-point correlations of supercurrents and supercurrents paired with superprimaries. Furthermore, we analyze the constraints imposed by superconformal symmetry on these functions in these distinct scenarios.

Children possess an innate drive to understand how the world functions, a trait that is especially pronounced in the digital age where they are constantly exposed to computers. While we have previously established that children naturally grasp the idea of machines executing step-by-step instructions, this study investigates whether this extends to recognizing that computer programs operate via sequential steps. To explore this, we introduced a new activity called "Machine Coding" to 4- to 5-year-olds, which they used to control a machine executing basic machine language commands. We found that children could quickly learn the machines and commands, and they were able to formulate and execute programs with ordered, sequential steps. However, they struggled with instructions that contained repeated loops or multiple branching paths. These findings suggest that while children naturally view computers as sequential processes capable of executing machine code, their capacity to handle more intricate programming structures remains limited.

Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has achieved significant breakthroughs in gaming, it remains unclear how to effectively apply these techniques to real-world industrial settings. This paper examines the practical challenges of deploying DRL in industry, focusing on three key areas: system longevity, the need for human oversight, and the difficulty of scaling. We argue that the primary obstacle to success lies in the system's design phase, where the most substantial challenges arise. We contend that the most critical step in the process is conceptualizing the problem, followed by designing a robust state representation. Furthermore, we emphasize that human oversight is indispensable for ensuring system longevity and scalability. Ultimately, we hope these insights will help industry practitioners navigate the complexities of implementing DRL in real-world applications.

We present an on-chip device capable of coherently converting optical quantum signals across varying degrees of freedom. Specifically, this system translates spatial quantum information into temporal degrees. We demonstrate that both classical and quantum signals can be efficiently converted with high fidelity. This system functions as a quantum interface, enabling the connection between integrated photonic chips and conventional fiber-optic infrastructure.

We investigate the quantum transport characteristics of DNA molecules, utilizing a tight-binding Hamiltonian that incorporates electron hopping, electron-phonon coupling, and the quantum nature of nucleobases. By applying the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, we demonstrate that the conductance of these molecules is significantly influenced by the presence of mispairs. This finding is further supported by a comparison of results derived from the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism.

This study introduces a new algorithm designed for the efficient and robust registration of multiple point clouds. The approach utilizes a modified K-means strategy to generate candidate correspondences, which are subsequently refined through a probabilistic model. The method is resilient to outliers, even when the point clouds are sparse. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of our algorithm, demonstrating that it requires only a linear number of operations relative to the size of the point clouds. The method's effectiveness is validated through experiments involving both real-world and synthetic data.

The Tb$^{3+}$ sublattice undergoes a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm SF} = 10.5$ K, while the Ru chains experience a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin-flop transition at $T_{\rm Sr} = 10.5$ K, followed by a spin

This study examines minimization problems subject to constraints within the framework of DC (difference of convex functions) and derives Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions for local optimality. The paper demonstrates that these KKT conditions are weak first-order optimality results. To further characterize local solutions, it introduces a refined local optimality condition, which serves as a second-order necessary condition. The authors also define a new local minimum definition for DC constrained mathematical programming problems (DCMPPs) and prove that this proposed notion aligns with the standard Bouligand minimum used in nonconvex programming.

We investigate the near-horizon limit of a D$(-1)/$D$7$ brane system, which is dual to a scalar field theory in $d=0$ dimensions. This theory features a quartic potential and a coupling that varies with the $x$ coordinate, where the coupling diverges as $x \to 0$. This specific setup is conjectured to represent the near-horizon limit of a $AdS_2$/CFT$_1$ duality. By analyzing the near-horizon limit of $AdS_2$, we derive a conjecture for the corresponding $AdS_0$/CFT$_0$ duality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the near-horizon limit of a $AdS_2$/CFT$_1$ theory can be mapped to a $AdS_0$/CFT$_0$ theory, thereby establishing a direct link between these two proposed dualities.

We introduce Domain Clashes, a novel logical framework that merges the rigid structure of classical first-order logic with the flexible nature of non-monotonic reasoning. In this system, a non-monotonic conclusion is deemed valid only if it remains consistent with every monotonic theory applicable to the premises under consideration. A theory is considered applicable when no other theory with a broader scope can be constructed without generating a clash. We establish that determining whether a non-monotonic conclusion is valid is co-Turing-complete, and that constructing such an applicable theory presents an exponential complexity challenge.

This paper presents a Bayesian controller integration (BCI) framework designed to embed model-based controllers within model-free policies, thereby improving sample efficiency in robotic tasks. The proposed method, termed Bayesian Controller Learning (BCL), treats the controller as a probabilistic prior during policy learning, which guides the agent toward optimal control parameters. We demonstrate that BCL can be implemented using a two-stage approach: first, training a policy via standard deep reinforcement learning, and second, refining it through Bayesian model averaging that weights model predictions against the controller prior. Empirical results on a simulated quadruped robot indicate that BCL outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by achieving faster convergence and superior performance.

This study introduces an end-to-end deep learning framework designed to enhance perfusion analysis in acute stroke patients. The approach utilizes computed tomography perfusion (CTP) data to generate a precise cerebral blood flow (CBF) map, which then serves as input for a perfusion analysis module. This module produces a perfusion map featuring a "core" region and a "penumbra" region. The entire system is optimized through a differentiable deconvolution process that relies on a custom loss function, trained using a large dataset of CTP images paired with ground-truth perfusion maps. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in both perfusion map generation and the accuracy of stroke perfusion analysis.

We present an investigation into the N$^3$LO QCD predictions for the zero-jettiness (z-jettiness) distribution of final-state jets produced in hadron-hadron collisions. Our analysis focuses on the specific case of two-jettiness, examining how the beam and underlying event influence this observable. By leveraging recent advancements in resummation theory, we demonstrate that the N$^3$LO soft function for two-jettiness can be reconstructed from data obtained from three-jettiness, thereby bypassing the need for explicit three-jettiness measurements. Furthermore, we derive a new leading-power result for the N$^3$LO soft function that incorporates beam and underlying event effects, which are crucial for accurately modeling the final-state jet z-jettiness. Finally, we provide comprehensive numerical predictions for the two-jettiness distribution, including scenarios with and without underlying event interactions.

This study examines $P(G)$, the group power graph associated with a finite group $G$, where vertices represent the group's elements and an edge connects two vertices if one is a power of the other. We demonstrate that if $G$ is cyclic, then $P(G)$ is chordal; however, if $G$ is non-cyclic, then $P(G)$ is chordal if and only if $G$ is isomorphic to a direct product of the form $C_2 \times C_2^k$ for some $k \geq 2$.

This study addresses the challenge of isolating a specific source within a noisy mixture. We introduce a new deep neural network designed to extract a signal of interest from such mixtures, leveraging a dedicated noise model. The architecture utilizes a deep encoder to capture the source signal's features and a deep decoder to reconstruct the target signal based on those features. The proposed model is trained using a specialized data generation process that creates a precise source-noise mixture along with the underlying source signal, thereby eliminating the need for noisy audio recorded in uncontrolled real-world settings. This optimal training approach yields superior performance compared to existing methods. The study also examines various model configurations, including different network depths and decoder types. The framework was implemented in PyTorch and made publicly available.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing consistency within quantum measurements. Our approach examines the compatibility between an initial state and a measurement outcome, establishing necessary and sufficient criteria for consistency across general quantum measurements. Specifically, we demonstrate that a quantum measurement on system $A$ is consistent with an initial state $\rho_A$ if and only if there exists a quantum channel for $A$ that maps $\rho_A$ to the post-measurement state $\rho_{A|x}$ corresponding to outcome $|x\rangle$, where $|x\rangle$ is an element of the measurement's outcome set. We report the discovery of Type C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in H 1743--322, a transient black hole X-ray binary, using data from the 2018 and 2019 outbursts captured by the NICER X-ray telescope. Our analysis reveals that the QPO frequency remains stable at approximately 1.1 Hz across multiple outbursts, with a consistent power spectral density profile. The QPO is characterized by a narrow peak at 1.1 Hz, accompanied by a low-frequency component around 0.1 Hz and a broad high-frequency feature centered at 10 Hz. The observed QPO amplitude is notably high, reaching 10--20% in the 2018 and 2019 outbursts. Based on the relationship between QPO frequency and black hole mass, we infer a mass of 10.8$^{+2.7}_{-2.2}$ M$_{\odot}$, which aligns with previous estimates. The presence of the QPO suggests that the accretion flow in H 1743--322 is dominated by a geometrically thick, optically thick disk. The high amplitude of the QPO indicates that the inner edge of the accretion flow is located close to the black hole, potentially near the marginally stable orbit.

This paper outlines a new, open-source Question Answering (QA) platform developed for the e-Governance sector, specifically designed to address the challenge of locating pertinent information within extensive document repositories. The system integrates a suite of modules for data ingestion, preprocessing, and content retrieval, along with a configurable, modular question encoding framework that employs fine-tuned pre-trained language models. Additionally, it includes a flexible system for answer retrieval and ranking. The platform supports both exact-matching retrieval and cross-lingual zero-shot QA capabilities. We also provide open-source implementations of various state-of-the-art model architectures for question encoders, alongside the integration of a ready-to-use UI for end-users.

This study examines the cosmic baryon cycle by analyzing the distribution of baryons across various phases—gas, circumgalactic medium (CGM), and stars—within the EAGLE simulation volume. A "divisor" of a string refers to a substring that divides evenly into the full string a whole number of times. We refer to a "divisor's leftmost occurrence" as its starting position within that total string. Our research focuses on the task of locating all divisors up to a specific size $k$ and identifying their leftmost instances. We demonstrate that this task can be solved in $O(n + o_p \log(o_p/ n))$ time, where $n$ represents the string's length and $o_p$ is the total count of divisors with size no greater than $k$.

We investigate the dynamical evolution of post-starburst (PSB) and Balmer-strong quiescent (QSO) galaxies by analyzing their velocity dispersion ($\sigma_e$), mass, and size. Our sample comprises 1,000 PSB galaxies and 1,000 QSOs, both drawn from the SDSS-DR12 catalog and selected using a specific $\sigma_e$-based method. We find that the $\sigma_e$ distributions for these groups are remarkably similar, with a median of 100 km/s and a standard deviation of 20 km/s. Consequently, the mass distributions for both populations are also nearly identical, with a median stellar mass of $10^{10.5} M_\odot$ and a dispersion of 0.2 dex. However, the QSOs exhibit a median size that is 0.1 dex larger than that of the PSBs. We categorize these galaxies into three distinct types based on their $\sigma_e$ values: Type I ($\sigma_e < 100$ km/s), Type II ($100 \leq \sigma_e < 120$ km/s), and Type III ($\sigma_e \geq 120$ km/s).
